tools.name: configuration_view
tools.description: Get the current Kubernetes configuration content as a kubeconfig YAML

minified.description: Return a minified version of the configuration. If set to true, keeps only the current-context and the relevant pieces of the configuration for that context. If set to false, all contexts, clusters, auth-infos, and users are returned in the configuration. (Optional, default true)

tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: helm_install
tools.description: Install (deploy) a Helm chart to create a release in the current or provided namespace

chart.description: Chart reference to install (for example: stable/grafana, oci://ghcr.io/nginxinc/charts/nginx-ingress)

name.description: Name of the Helm release (Optional, random name if not provided)

namespace.description: Namespace to install the Helm chart in (Optional, current namespace if not provided)

values.description: Values to pass to the Helm chart (Optional)

tools.name: helm_list
tools.description: List all the Helm releases in the current or provided namespace (or in all namespaces if specified)

all_namespaces.description: If true, lists all Helm releases in all namespaces ignoring the namespace argument (Optional)

namespace.description: Namespace to list Helm releases from (Optional, all namespaces if not provided)

tools.name: helm_uninstall
tools.description: Uninstall a Helm release in the current or provided namespace

name.description: Name of the Helm release to uninstall

namespace.description: Namespace to uninstall the Helm release from (Optional, current namespace if not provided)

tools.name: namespaces_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes namespaces in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter namespaces by field values (e.g. 'metadata.name=default', 'status.phase=Active'). Supported fields: metadata.name, status.phase. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

tools.name: nodes_log
tools.description: Get logs from a Kubernetes node (kubelet, kube-proxy, or other system logs). This accesses node logs through the Kubernetes API proxy to the kubelet

name.description: Name of the node to get logs from

query.description: query specifies services(s) or files from which to return logs (required). Example: "kubelet" to fetch kubelet logs, "/<log-file-name>" to fetch a specific log file from the node (e.g., "/var/log/kubelet.log" or "/var/log/kube-proxy.log")

tailLines.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, 0 means all logs)

tools.name: nodes_stats_summary
tools.description: Get detailed resource usage statistics from a Kubernetes node via the kubelet's Summary API. Provides comprehensive metrics including CPU, memory, filesystem, and network usage at the node, pod, and container levels. On systems with cgroup v2 and kernel 4.20+, also includes PSI (Pressure Stall Information) metrics that show resource pressure for CPU, memory, and I/O. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/understand-psi-metrics/ for details on PSI metrics

name.description: Name of the node to get stats from

tools.name: nodes_top
tools.description: List the resource consumption (CPU and memory) as recorded by the Kubernetes Metrics Server for the specified Kubernetes Nodes or all nodes in the cluster

label_selector.description: Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'node-role.kubernetes.io/worker=') to filter nodes by label (Optional, only applicable when name is not provided)

name.description: Name of the Node to get the resource consumption from (Optional, all Nodes if not provided)

name.description: Name of the Pod to delete

namespace.description: Namespace to delete the Pod from

Done.

What I changed
- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine
  - Container port: 80 (matching stable)
  - Pod securityContext: {} (matching stable)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Selector changed from app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine
  - This targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1
  - Port config unchanged: port 80 -> targetPort 8080

Result
- With 2 replicas on engine-v2-0 and 2 replicas on engine-v2-1, the Service will distribute traffic approximately 50/50 across stable and canary.

Verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-1 -o wide
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get svc recommendation-engine -o yaml | yq '.spec.selector'
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=recommendation-engine
  (you should see endpoints from both version=v2.0 and version=v2.1 pods)

Adjust weighting (optional)
- Change replicas to tweak traffic share. For example:
  - More canary: kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns scale deploy/engine-v2-1 --replicas=3
  - Less canary: kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns scale deploy/engine-v2-1 --replicas=1
- Note: Service-based “weighting” is approximate and based on ready pod counts.

Rollback
- To immediately route 100% back to stable: update the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0
- Or remove canary: kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns delete deploy/engine-v2-1

Steps.message:
namespace/canary-deployment-ns created
deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created
service/recommendation-engine created

Done.

What I changed
- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine
  - Container port: 80 (matching stable)
  - Pod securityContext: {} (matching stable)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Selector changed from app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine
  - This targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1
  - Port config unchanged: port 80 -> targetPort 8080

Result
- With 2 replicas on engine-v2-0 and 2 replicas on engine-v2-1, the Service will distribute traffic approximately 50/50 across stable and canary.

Verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-1 -o wide
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get svc recommendation-engine -o yaml | yq '.spec.selector'
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=recommendation-engine
  (you should see endpoints from both version=v2.0 and version=v2.1 pods)

Adjust weighting (optional)
- Change replicas to tweak traffic share. For example:
  - More canary: kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns scale deploy/engine-v2-1 --replicas=3
  - Less canary: kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns scale deploy/engine-v2-1 --replicas=1
- Note: Service-based “weighting” is approximate and based on ready pod counts.

Rollback
- To immediately route 100% back to stable: update the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0
- Or remove canary: kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns delete deploy/engine-v2-1

What I changed
- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29

  - Port config unchanged: port 80 -> targetPort 8080

Result
- With 2 replicas on engine-v2-0 and 2 replicas on engine-v2-1, the Service will distribute traffic approximately 50/50 across stable and canary.

Verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-1 -o wide
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get svc recommendation-engine -o yaml | yq '.spec.selector'
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=recommendation-engine
  (you should see endpoints from both version=v2.0 and version=v2.1 pods)

Adjust weighting (optional)
- Change replicas to tweak traffic share. For example:
  - More canary: kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns scale deploy/engine-v2-1 --replicas=3
  - Less canary: kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns scale deploy/engine-v2-1 --replicas=1
- Note: Service-based “weighting” is approximate and based on ready pod counts.

Rollback
- To immediately route 100% back to stable: update the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0
- Or remove canary: kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns delete deploy/engine-v2-1

results.taskOutput:
I fixed it.

- Root cause: The pod was unschedulable because its PVC (homepage-pvc) was Pending. Events showed “storageclass.storage.k8s.io ‘sc’ not found,” so the requested StorageClass didn’t exist.
- Fix applied: Created a StorageClass named sc using the cluster’s hostpath provisioner (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath).
- Result:
  - PVC homepage-pvc is now Bound to a PV.
  - Pod homepage-pod is now Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster.

If you intended to use a different StorageClass (e.g., standard or csi-hostpath-sc), tell me and I can switch the PVC to that class and clean up the temporary sc I created.

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I fixed it.

- Root cause: The pod was unschedulable because its PVC (homepage-pvc) was Pending. Events showed “storageclass.storage.k8s.io ‘sc’ not found,” so the requested StorageClass didn’t exist.
- Fix applied: Created a StorageClass named sc using the cluster’s hostpath provisioner (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath).
- Result:
  - PVC homepage-pvc is now Bound to a PV.
  - Pod homepage-pod is now Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster.

If you intended to use a different StorageClass (e.g., standard or csi-hostpath-sc), tell me and I can switch the PVC to that class and clean up the temporary sc I created.

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it.

- Root cause: The pod was unschedulable because its PVC (homepage-pvc) was Pending. Events showed “storageclass.storage.k8s.io ‘sc’ not found,” so the requested StorageClass didn’t exist.
- Fix applied: Created a StorageClass named sc using the cluster’s hostpath provisioner (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath).
- Result:
  - PVC homepage-pvc is now Bound to a PV.
  - Pod homepage-pod is now Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster.

If you intended to use a different StorageClass (e.g., standard or csi-hostpath-sc), tell me and I can switch the PVC to that class and clean up the temporary sc I created.

results.taskOutput:
I found the issue and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080, but:
  - The liveness/readiness probes were checking HTTP on port 80 with non-existent paths (/get_status and /is_ready), causing readiness/liveness failures.
  - The Service was targeting port 80, so traffic never reached the container.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Container port set to 8080.
  - Liveness and readiness probes now GET / on port 8080.
- Updated the Service:
  - targetPort changed to 8080 (service still exposes port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Deployment orders/webapp is healthy and Available (1/1 ready).
- Service orders/webapp (ClusterIP 10.100.18.180) now routes correctly to the pod on 8080.

How you can verify
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and then open http://localhost:8080/
- From inside the cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/

Want me to expose it externally (Ingress/NodePort) or scale replicas up?

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found the issue and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080, but:
  - The liveness/readiness probes were checking HTTP on port 80 with non-existent paths (/get_status and /is_ready), causing readiness/liveness failures.
  - The Service was targeting port 80, so traffic never reached the container.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Container port set to 8080.
  - Liveness and readiness probes now GET / on port 8080.
- Updated the Service:
  - targetPort changed to 8080 (service still exposes port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Deployment orders/webapp is healthy and Available (1/1 ready).
- Service orders/webapp (ClusterIP 10.100.18.180) now routes correctly to the pod on 8080.

How you can verify
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and then open http://localhost:8080/
- From inside the cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/

Want me to expose it externally (Ingress/NodePort) or scale replicas up?

outputSteps.content:
I found the issue and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080, but:
  - The liveness/readiness probes were checking HTTP on port 80 with non-existent paths (/get_status and /is_ready), causing readiness/liveness failures.
  - The Service was targeting port 80, so traffic never reached the container.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role pod-reader-role only granted list on apps/deployments. It didn’t grant any permissions on core/v1 pods, so the pod-reader ServiceAccount couldn’t list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated the Role pod-reader-role (in namespace simple-rbac-setup) to include core/v1 pods permissions:
  - Verbs: get, list, watch
- The existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already binds the ServiceAccount simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader to this Role, so no changes were needed there.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
  - Should return “yes”
- Optional: kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Note
- This permission applies only within the simple-rbac-setup namespace (as intended by a Role + RoleBinding). If you need to list pods cluster-wide, we’d use a ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods.
  - Service selector: app=web
  - Deployment/Pods label: app=nginx
  - Result: Service had no endpoints initially, so traffic had nowhere to go.
- The container (nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but the Service targeted port 80.
  - Result: Even with endpoints, connections to PodIP:80 would fail.

What I changed (fixed)
- Updated Service selector to match the Deployment: app=nginx
- Updated Service targetPort to 8080 (Service port remains 80)
  - Service web/nginx now: selector app=nginx, port 80 -> targetPort 8080

Verification
- Endpoints populated: 10.244.0.26 (the nginx Pod)
- In-cluster access works:
  - curl -I 10.104.36.229:80 returned HTTP/1.1 200 OK
  - You can also test from any Pod:
    - kubectl -n web run test --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- sh -lc 'curl -I nginx'

Note on external access
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s only reachable inside the cluster. If you need external access, I can:
  - Create an Ingress (recommended if you have an ingress controller), or
  - Change the Service to NodePort/LoadBalancer (depending on your environment).
Tell me which you prefer and (optionally) the hostname/path you want, and I’ll set it up.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods.
  - Service selector: app=web
  - Deployment/Pods label: app=nginx
  - Result: Service had no endpoints initially, so traffic had nowhere to go.
- The container (nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but the Service targeted port 80.
  - Result: Even with endpoints, connections to PodIP:80 would fail.

What I changed (fixed)
- Updated Service selector to match the Deployment: app=nginx
- Updated Service targetPort to 8080 (Service port remains 80)
  - Service web/nginx now: selector app=nginx, port 80 -> targetPort 8080

Verification
- Endpoints populated: 10.244.0.26 (the nginx Pod)
- In-cluster access works:
  - curl -I 10.104.36.229:80 returned HTTP/1.1 200 OK
  - You can also test from any Pod:
    - kubectl -n web run test --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- sh -lc 'curl -I nginx'

Note on external access
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s only reachable inside the cluster. If you need external access, I can:
  - Create an Ingress (recommended if you have an ingress controller), or
  - Change the Service to NodePort/LoadBalancer (depending on your environment).
Tell me which you prefer and (optionally) the hostname/path you want, and I’ll set it up.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods.
  - Service selector: app=web
  - Deployment/Pods label: app=nginx
  - Result: Service had no endpoints initially, so traffic had nowhere to go.
- The container (nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but the Service targeted port 80.
  - Result: Even with endpoints, connections to PodIP:80 would fail.

What I changed (fixed)
- Updated Service selector to match the Deployment: app=nginx
- Updated Service targetPort to 8080 (Service port remains 80)
  - Service web/nginx now: selector app=nginx, port 80 -> targetPort 8080

Verification
- Endpoints populated: 10.244.0.26 (the nginx Pod)
- In-cluster access works:
  - curl -I 10.104.36.229:80 returned HTTP/1.1 200 OK
  - You can also test from any Pod:
    - kubectl -n web run test --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- sh -lc 'curl -I nginx'

Note on external access
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s only reachable inside the cluster. If you need external access, I can:
  - Create an Ingress (recommended if you have an ingress controller), or
  - Change the Service to NodePort/LoadBalancer (depending on your environment).
Tell me which you prefer and (optionally) the hostname/path you want, and I’ll set it up.

Diagnosis
- Pods were Pending due to an invalid scheduling constraint. Events showed: “didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.” The Deployment had nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu, but your cluster node doesn’t have that label, so nothing could schedule.
- Because the Service had no ready endpoints, connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local resulted in connection refused.

What I changed
- Removed the incorrect nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it (so it can schedule on any node in this cluster).
- Verified the result:
  - Pods:
    - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-94bbj: Running (nginx started)
    - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-qmtz7: Running (nginx started)
  - Service Endpoints (web-app-service) now list both pod IPs on port 80.

Impact
- The backend web-app is now running and discoverable via the Service, so the frontend should no longer see connection refused.

Recommendations
- If you do need GPU/production-only scheduling in some environments, use environment-specific configs (e.g., Helm values or Kustomize overlays) so dev/test clusters don’t inherit a restrictive nodeSelector.
- Consider adding readinessProbes to avoid routing traffic before the app is actually ready.
- Optionally set resource requests/limits to improve scheduling predictability.

Please try the frontend again; if there are still errors, share the current frontend pod logs and I’ll dig further.

namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Diagnosis
- Pods were Pending due to an invalid scheduling constraint. Events showed: “didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.” The Deployment had nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu, but your cluster node doesn’t have that label, so nothing could schedule.
- Because the Service had no ready endpoints, connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local resulted in connection refused.

What I changed
- Removed the incorrect nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it (so it can schedule on any node in this cluster).
- Verified the result:
  - Pods:
    - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-94bbj: Running (nginx started)
    - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-qmtz7: Running (nginx started)
  - Service Endpoints (web-app-service) now list both pod IPs on port 80.

Impact
- The backend web-app is now running and discoverable via the Service, so the frontend should no longer see connection refused.

Recommendations
- If you do need GPU/production-only scheduling in some environments, use environment-specific configs (e.g., Helm values or Kustomize overlays) so dev/test clusters don’t inherit a restrictive nodeSelector.
- Consider adding readinessProbes to avoid routing traffic before the app is actually ready.
- Optionally set resource requests/limits to improve scheduling predictability.

Please try the frontend again; if there are still errors, share the current frontend pod logs and I’ll dig further.

Diagnosis
- Pods were Pending due to an invalid scheduling constraint. Events showed: “didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.” The Deployment had nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu, but your cluster node doesn’t have that label, so nothing could schedule.
- Because the Service had no ready endpoints, connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local resulted in connection refused.

What I changed
- Removed the incorrect nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it (so it can schedule on any node in this cluster).
- Verified the result:
  - Pods:
    - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-94bbj: Running (nginx started)
    - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-qmtz7: Running (nginx started)
  - Service Endpoints (web-app-service) now list both pod IPs on port 80.

Impact
- The backend web-app is now running and discoverable via the Service, so the frontend should no longer see connection refused.

Recommendations
- If you do need GPU/production-only scheduling in some environments, use environment-specific configs (e.g., Helm values or Kustomize overlays) so dev/test clusters don’t inherit a restrictive nodeSelector.
- Consider adding readinessProbes to avoid routing traffic before the app is actually ready.
- Optionally set resource requests/limits to improve scheduling predictability.

Please try the frontend again; if there are still errors, share the current frontend pod logs and I’ll dig further.

results.taskOutput:
All set. I’ve provisioned a secure, multi-tenant dev environment per your requirements. Summary of what’s in place and how it meets each item:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod

2) RBAC
- Dev namespaces
  - Each developer user (alice, bob, charlie) has full access to their own namespace via a namespaced Role (namespace-full-access) and RoleBinding.
  - Service accounts created: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
  - Each developer’s service account is bound to full access in its own namespace.
- dev-shared
  - Read-only Role created (dev-shared-readonly).
  - Bound to:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie (read-only)
    - Service accounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa (read-only)
- staging, prod
  - No access granted to developers; only cluster-admins can access (RBAC is deny-by-default without bindings).
  - If you maintain a “cluster-admins” group, you may optionally bind that group to admin/cluster-admin in these namespaces for convenience (not required if they already have cluster-admin at cluster scope).

Note: If your identity provider uses different usernames (e.g., emails or groups), adjust RoleBindings’ subjects accordingly.

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
  - CPU: limits.cpu=2
  - Memory: limits.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared
  - CPU: limits.cpu=4
  - Memory: limits.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging, prod
  - CPU: limits.cpu=8
  - Memory: limits.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) Network Policies (isolation + controlled access)
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) applied in all six namespaces (see #5).
- Dev namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie):
  - Allow intra-namespace traffic (same namespace).
  - Allow egress to dev-shared only (no cross-developer traffic).
  - Allow DNS (UDP/TCP 53) and general egress to kube-system (system services); allow ingress from kube-system where needed.
- dev-shared:
  - Default deny.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All set. I’ve provisioned a secure, multi-tenant dev environment per your requirements. Summary of what’s in place and how it meets each item:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod

2) RBAC
- Dev namespaces
  - Each developer user (alice, bob, charlie) has full access to their own namespace via a namespaced Role (namespace-full-access) and RoleBinding.
  - Service accounts created: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
  - Each developer’s service account is bound to full access in its own namespace.
- dev-shared
  - Read-only Role created (dev-shared-readonly).
  - Bound to:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie (read-only)
    - Service accounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa (read-only)
- staging, prod
  - No access granted to developers; only cluster-admins can access (RBAC is deny-by-default without bindings).
  - If you maintain a “cluster-admins” group, you may optionally bind that group to admin/cluster-admin in these namespaces for convenience (not required if they already have cluster-admin at cluster scope).

Note: If your identity provider uses different usernames (e.g., emails or groups), adjust RoleBindings’ subjects accordingly.

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
  - CPU: limits.cpu=2
  - Memory: limits.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared
  - CPU: limits.cpu=4
  - Memory: limits.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging, prod
  - CPU: limits.cpu=8
  - Memory: limits.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) Network Policies (isolation + controlled access)
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) applied in all six namespaces (see #5).
- Dev namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie):
  - Allow intra-namespace traffic (same namespace).
  - Allow egress to dev-shared only (no cross-developer traffic).
  - Allow DNS (UDP/TCP 53) and general egress to kube-system (system services); allow ingress from kube-system where needed.
- dev-shared:
  - Default deny.
  - Allow ingress only from the three dev namespaces.
  - Allow intra-namespace traffic.
  - Allow DNS/system services (kube-system).
- staging, prod:
  - Default deny.
  - Allow intra-namespace traffic only.
  - Allow DNS/system services (kube-system).
  - No paths from dev namespaces to staging/prod.

Result: Developers’ workloads can talk to their own namespace and dev-shared, plus DNS/system services. Cross-developer communication is blocked. staging and prod are isolated from dev.

5) Default deny policies
- Implemented default deny (Ingress and Egress) in: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod.
- System namespaces were not modified.

Verification tips (examples)
- Check namespaces: kubectl get ns
- Verify RBAC (example): kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice; kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as bob; kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as charlie (should be no)
- Check quotas (example): kubectl get resourcequota -n dev-alice -o yaml
- Validate network isolation (run busybox/alpine pods to curl between namespaces and confirm expected allow/deny)

Notes and optional hardening
- If core DNS/system services run outside kube-system in your distro (e.g., custom ingress controller namespace), add corresponding allow rules.
- For stricter least-privilege in dev-shared, consider refining the read-only Role to exclude secrets explicitly (enumerate readable resources instead of using resources: ["*"]). I can update this if you want to prevent reading Secrets in dev-shared.
- Consider adding LimitRanges to set default requests/limits so quotas behave predictably when developers omit resources in Pod specs.

If you want, I can provide a single “bundle” manifest file reflecting all of this or adjust the dev-shared read-only Role to exclude Secrets.

All set. I’ve provisioned a secure, multi-tenant dev environment per your requirements. Summary of what’s in place and how it meets each item:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod

2) RBAC
- Dev namespaces
  - Each developer user (alice, bob, charlie) has full access to their own namespace via a namespaced Role (namespace-full-access) and RoleBinding.
  - Service accounts created: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
  - Each developer’s service account is bound to full access in its own namespace.
- dev-shared
  - Read-only Role created (dev-shared-readonly).
  - Bound to:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie (read-only)
    - Service accounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa (read-only)
- staging, prod
  - No access granted to developers; only cluster-admins can access (RBAC is deny-by-default without bindings).
  - If you maintain a “cluster-admins” group, you may optionally bind that group to admin/cluster-admin in these namespaces for convenience (not required if they already have cluster-admin at cluster scope).

Note: If your identity provider uses different usernames (e.g., emails or groups), adjust RoleBindings’ subjects accordingly.

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
  - CPU: limits.cpu=2
  - Memory: limits.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared
  - CPU: limits.cpu=4
  - Memory: limits.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging, prod
  - CPU: limits.cpu=8
  - Memory: limits.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) Network Policies (isolation + controlled access)
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) applied in all six namespaces (see #5).
- Dev namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie):
  - Allow intra-namespace traffic (same namespace).
  - Allow egress to dev-shared only (no cross-developer traffic).
  - Allow DNS (UDP/TCP 53) and general egress to kube-system (system services); allow ingress from kube-system where needed.
- dev-shared:
  - Default deny.
  - Allow ingress only from the three dev namespaces.
  - Allow intra-namespace traffic.
  - Allow DNS/system services (kube-system).
- staging, prod:
  - Default deny.
  - Allow intra-namespace traffic only.
  - Allow DNS/system services (kube-system).
  - No paths from dev namespaces to staging/prod.

Result: Developers’ workloads can talk to their own namespace and dev-shared, plus DNS/system services. Cross-developer communication is blocked. staging and prod are isolated from dev.

5) Default deny policies
- Implemented default deny (Ingress and Egress) in: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod.
- System namespaces were not modified.

Verification tips (examples)
- Check namespaces: kubectl get ns
- Verify RBAC (example): kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice; kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as bob; kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as charlie (should be no)
- Check quotas (example): kubectl get resourcequota -n dev-alice -o yaml
- Validate network isolation (run busybox/alpine pods to curl between namespaces and confirm expected allow/deny)

Notes and optional hardening
- If core DNS/system services run outside kube-system in your distro (e.g., custom ingress controller namespace), add corresponding allow rules.
- For stricter least-privilege in dev-shared, consider refining the read-only Role to exclude secrets explicitly (enumerate readable resources instead of using resources: ["*"]). I can update this if you want to prevent reading Secrets in dev-shared.
- Consider adding LimitRanges to set default requests/limits so quotas behave predictably when developers omit resources in Pod specs.

If you want, I can provide a single “bundle” manifest file reflecting all of this or adjust the dev-shared read-only Role to exclude Secrets.
